pages.title: U.S. corn-based ethanol worse for the climate than gasoline, study finds

topClaims.text: Corn-based ethanol is likely at least **24% more carbon-intensive than gasoline** due to emissions from land use changes, processing, and combustion. [evidence: PNAS study, funded by National Wildlife Federation and U.S. Department of Energy]
The study **contradicts previous USDA research** (2019) that found ethanol's carbon intensity was 39% lower than gasoline — partly because USDA underestimated the emissions impact of land conversion.

The **Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS)**, enacted in 2005, requires ~15 billion gallons of corn ethanol blended into U.S. gasoline annually. As a result, **corn cultivation grew 8.7%** and expanded into **6.9 million additional acres** (2008–2016).
Land use changes triggered by ethanol demand include tilling retired/conservation cropland, which releases soil carbon, and increased nitrogen fertilizer use.
The EPA is considering reforms to the RFS program, with authority to set 2023 requirements in May 2022 (Congress set mandates only through 2022).
